title: Evaluation Functions, Expectimax & MCTS
html:
Real games are too big to search to the end. Engines stop at a depth limit and estimate the position; games with dice need expectation instead of minimum; and Monte Carlo tree search replaces hand-made evaluation with random playouts.

Depth cut-off and evaluation functions

Replace IsTerminal with a cut-off test (depth limit, or time) and Utility with an evaluation function — an estimate of the expected utility of a position. Most classical engines use a weighted linear sum of features:

Eval(s) = w₁·f₁(s) + w₂·f₂(s) + … + wₙ·fₙ(s)
ProblemWhat goes wrongRemedy
Horizon effectA delaying move pushes an unavoidable loss beyond the depth limit, so the engine thinks it is avoidedSingular extensions — search forcing moves deeper
Non-quiescent positionsCutting off in the middle of a capture sequence gives a wildly wrong estimateQuiescence search — keep searching captures until the position is quiet
Weights are hand-tunedThe evaluation encodes human biases and misses deep strategyLearn the evaluation (TD-Gammon, AlphaZero value networks)

Expectimax — games of chance

In backgammon a dice roll sits between the players' moves. Add chance nodes whose value is the probability-weighted average of their children:

EXPECTIMINIMAX(s) = Σ over outcomes r of P(r) · EXPECTIMINIMAX(Result(s, r)) at chance nodes
Watch out

With chance nodes the scale of the evaluation matters, not just the ranking: only a positive linear transformation of the true expected payoff preserves the best move. Minimax is indifferent to any order-preserving transformation.

Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS)

MCTS needs no evaluation function: it estimates a position's value by playing many (quick, often random) games to the end, and grows a search tree focused on the most promising moves. Each iteration has four steps:

1 · Selection (follow UCB1 down the tree)
→
2 · Expansion (add one new child)
→
3 · Simulation (random playout to the end)
→
4 · Backpropagation (update wins/visits up the path)
UCB1(n) = W(n)/N(n) + C · √( ln N(parent) / N(n) ) exploitation + exploration, C ≈ √2

Demo on Nim: 10 sticks, each turn take 1–3, whoever takes the last stick wins. The winning strategy is to leave the opponent a multiple of 4 — so from 10 the right move is to take 2. MCTS discovers this from random playouts alone:

Alpha-beta + evaluationMCTS
NeedsA good hand-crafted (or learned) evaluation functionOnly the rules (to simulate) — any-time
Good forTactical games with moderate b (chess, checkers)Huge b, hard-to-evaluate positions (Go: b ≈ 250)
Search shapeUniform to a fixed depthAsymmetric — deep on promising lines
Famous useDeep Blue (1997), StockfishAlphaGo / AlphaZero (MCTS + policy and value networks)
Key point

AlphaZero replaced random playouts with a value network and biased selection with a policy network, both trained by self-play reinforcement learning — search and learning working together (see Reinforcement Learning and the Deep Learning notes).

What is the horizon effect?

A depth-limited search can't see consequences beyond its cut-off, so an engine may play delaying moves that merely push an inevitable loss past the horizon. Quiescence search and search extensions reduce it.

When would you use expectimax instead of minimax?

When outcomes involve chance (dice, card draws) or the opponent is not adversarial but random/suboptimal. Chance nodes take the probability-weighted average of their children instead of the minimum.

Explain the four phases of MCTS.

Selection: descend the tree choosing children by UCB1 (balancing win rate and uncertainty). Expansion: add a new child node. Simulation: play out the game from there with a default (often random) policy. Backpropagation: update visit and win counts along the path. The move with the most visits at the root is played.
